Maladaptive Strategies.value: go along with whatever others want to feel safe
Being alone in a room or building
Crowded places such as shopping centres or public events

Threat.value: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
The people responsible have faced no consequences
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

issues.item: Threat: Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, nocturnal checking for one's own immediate physical safety is not impossible, but paired with the rest of the profile it introduces a more direct personal-danger threat theme that is not otherwise represented in triggers or memory. The triggers and memory items are centered on reminders of the loved one's trauma/loss rather than the patient's own current physical danger, so this specific item is the least coherent threat item.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am
issues.explanation: Self-blame based on one's character can occur after a loved one's trauma, but here it sits awkwardly beside appraisals focused on institutional failure and lack of accountability, which externalize blame to others. This is not impossible, but this item is the most internally tensioned within the appraisal node and less clearly linked to the rest of the profile than guilt on recall would be.

vignette: Tariq was fifty-two when he finally walked into a clinic, but the weight of his symptoms had been building for nearly a decade. It began at the old Meridian Theatre, during a dress rehearsal where a collapsed lighting grid killed his younger brother, Layth. Tariq had been in the front row, watching as steel cables snapped without warning. The event never played out as a continuous narrative for him; instead, he experienced photographic recalls of Layth pinned beneath the wreckage, followed instantly by fragmented pieces of scattered rigging and his brother's stunned face. When those disconnected images surfaced with their accompanying guilt, Tariq felt compelled to surrender his own boundaries, going along with whatever his directors or casting agents demanded just to feel momentarily safe, while his isolation in empty rooms only allowed the memories to replay louder. Digging through the aftermath, he learned the theater company had buried hazard reports and quietly signed off on the equipment. The official inquiry cleared everyone. No accountability was ever pursued, and Tariq had come to believe the institutions that should have protected them had fundamentally let him down. Over the following months, ordinary stimuli became relentless entry points into that trauma. A radio news segment about a venue fire would instantly pull him back to the Meridian, conjuring the same flash-like memories of the collapse. Even subtle auditory cues-a dropped set piece, a sudden clatter backstage, or the distant wail of a child in a grocery aisle-sped up his pulse and triggered those photographic flashes. These sensory shocks did not stop at fear; they cemented his conviction that the institutions guarding public spaces were fundamentally compromised, locking his inaction guilt in place. Because his negative emotions and inability to trust safety ran so high, he became hyper-vigilant to media and ambient sounds, which in turn sparked the next wave of panic. When the sensory shocks spiked his heart rate, Tariq felt forced to flee crowded venues like shopping centers or public theaters, telling himself these habits were just career boundaries when they were really flight responses to a threat system that could not be switched off. The avoidance and appeasement only sharpened his internal alarm. Every time the memories surfaced, the guilt on recall tightened his chest, and the negative emotions that followed-horror, shame, and paralyzing fear-made it impossible for him to concentrate on script lines. Because he could not trust that safety was real, even when agents swore the new inspections were thorough, Tariq felt compelled to avoid being alone in any room or building after dark. The negative appraisals of institutional failure and inaction guilt compounded the threat; if the system had abandoned Layth once, it would abandon him too, and he would be forever responsible for not preventing it. The paralysis of fear and shame reinforced his belief that the system had failed them and would never change, while continuing to appease everyone and avoid crowds only convinced him that he lacked the agency to demand justice, reinforcing his negative appraisal that no accountability would ever come. At fifty-two, the loop had become the architecture of his days. A director's casual mention of "the old warehouse stage" would trigger a cascade: the memory of Layth's pinned shoulder would flash, the inability to trust safety would spike his heart rate, and the conviction that the system had abandoned them once would lock his throat shut. His constant people-pleasing had cost him his marriage; his late wife had left years ago, unable to tolerate a husband who flinched at children crying in the grocery aisle or who refused to share a quiet dinner alone. The fewer crowds he navigated, the less tolerance he had for unexpected noise, meaning everyday background sounds suddenly felt as dangerous as the collapse itself. This constant hypervigilance kept his concentration shattered and his guilt and shame at a boil, making safety feel perpetually out of reach while the cycle fed on itself. What finally brought him to a clinic was a near-collapse during a monologue rehearsal, where the lights dimmed and he was certain the grid was groaning again. He sought help not to forget Layth, but to break the suffocating cycle where every sound, every crowd, and every quiet moment only proved to him that the world was unsafe, the system was corrupt, and his guilt was a permanent sentence.
